questions.title: How exactly does the Cayley transform guarantee orthogonality in BOFT?
questions.question_body: The paper uses the Cayley parameterization \(\mathbf{R}=(\mathbf{I}+\mathbf{Q})(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q})^{-1}\) with \(\mathbf{Q}=-\mathbf{Q}^\top\) to ensure orthogonality for each butterfly component. I understand that for skew-symmetric \(\mathbf{Q}\), \(\mathbf{R}\) is orthogonal when \(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q}\) is invertible. But I'm confused about: (1) Are there conditions under which \(\mathbf{I}-\mathbf{Q}\) can become nearly singular during training (leading to numerical instability)? (2) Since each butterfly component is a block permutation of \(2\times 2\) (or \(2b\times 2b\)) orthogonal blocks, do we apply a separate Cayley transform to each small block, or a single Cayley to the full sparse matrix? (3) Does this parameterization cover all of \(O(d)\) or just a subset (because Cayley misses matrices with eigenvalue \(-1\)) and how is that handled in practice?

questions.title: Deriving the parameter count \(\tfrac{1}{2}(b-1)dm\) for BOFT(m, b)
questions.question_body: The paper states that BOFT(\(m,b\)) "takes \(\tfrac{1}{2}(b-1)dm\) effective trainable parameters for finetuning a linear layer of size \(d\times n\)." Could someone provide a step-by-step derivation? Specifically: (1) For a single butterfly component with block size \(2b\times 2b\), how many free parameters does one orthogonal block have? (2) How many such blocks exist per component at width \(d\)? (3) How does orthogonality reduce the parameter count compared to counting nonzeros? (4) Why does multiplying by \(m\) components give the \(\tfrac{1}{2}(b-1)dm\) figure?

questions.title: What does “effective trainable parameters” mean when edges are constrained by orthogonality?
questions.question_body: In the information transmission view, the paper counts "free edges" and notes that orthogonality implies dependencies (e.g., in a \(2\times 2\) orthogonal matrix, one zero forces another zero). How should I interpret the statement that some edges "are not trainable" (e.g., must be \(\pm 1\))? Is there a formal mapping from edges to parameters after imposing orthogonality constraints, and how does this mapping yield the final parameter count?

questions.title: How does the butterfly factorization ensure dense connectivity with only \(\mathcal{O}(d\log d)\) parameters?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that stacking \(m=\log d\) butterfly components gives a dense orthogonal matrix \(\mathbf{R}\) using \(\mathcal{O}(d\log d)\) parameters. Could someone explain in graph-theoretic terms why every source node can reach every sink node after \(\log d\) butterfly layers? A small worked example for \(d=8\) would be very helpful.

questions.title: Relationship between BOFT(m, b) and OFT: Why is m=1 equivalent to block-diagonal OFT(b)?
questions.question_body: The paper states BOFT(1, b) reduces to block-diagonal OFT with block size \(b\). I’m missing the exact correspondence: (1) How does a single butterfly component with block size \(b\) reduce to a block-diagonal orthogonal transform? (2) Are permutations disabled in the \(m=1\) case, or do they cancel out? A concrete illustration for \(d=8\), \(b=2\) would clarify.

questions.title: How do we implement BOFT when \(d\) is not a power of two?
questions.question_body: The construction assumes \(d=2^N\). In practice, layers often have widths like 768 or 3072. What are the recommended strategies: padding to the next power of two, mixed-radix butterfly, or grouping into near-equal powers with permutations? How does each choice affect orthogonality, parameter count, and runtime?

questions.title: Is the BOFT dropout (replacing sub-blocks by identity) unbiased and does it preserve orthogonality?
questions.question_body: The multiplicative Dropout randomly picks a subset of butterfly components and diagonal blocks within components and replaces those sub-blocks by identities. (1) Is the resulting matrix exactly orthogonal during training when some sub-blocks are identity and others are learned? (2) Is there an argument that the expected transformed weight equals the un-dropped case under some scaling (like standard Dropout)? (3) How does this interact with the Cayley parameterization and gradient flow through inactive (identity) sub-blocks?

questions.title: Expressivity theorem: How does the kaleidoscope hierarchy span the full orthogonal group?
questions.question_body: Theorem 1 mentions that multiplying a sequence of butterfly matrices \(\mathbf{B}_{i,1}(d)\mathbf{B}_{i,2}(d)^\top\) for \(i=1,\dots,d-1\) can represent all orthogonal matrices. Could someone sketch or reference a proof? Specifically: (1) What are the key properties of butterfly matrices that allow this spanning? (2) Is there a constructive procedure to decompose any \(\mathbf{R}\in O(d)\) into that product? (3) How does the depth and parameter count compare with Givens or Householder factorizations that are known to generate \(O(d)\)?

questions.title: Comparing BOFT with Givens/Householder: Are we just choosing a different sparse orthogonal basis?
questions.question_body: Classical linear algebra provides parameter-efficient orthogonal factorizations using Givens rotations (sparse with \(2\times 2\) active sub-blocks) or Householder reflections. BOFT also uses products of sparse orthogonals arranged in a butterfly pattern. How does BOFT’s expressivity, parameter sharing, and computational layout compare to (a) a schedule of Givens rotations and (b) a sequence of Householder reflectors, under similar parameter budgets and parallelism constraints?

questions.title: Spectral norm preservation: Is \(\lVert \mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0\rVert_2=\lVert \mathbf{W}^0\rVert_2\) always true for BOFT?
questions.question_body: The paper argues that BOFT preserves the spectral norm since it left-multiplies by an orthogonal \(\mathbf{R}\). Is there any caveat due to finite precision or the Cayley transform’s numerical errors? Also, does the same argument imply that all singular values are preserved if \(\mathbf{R}\) multiplies on the left (i.e., only the left singular vectors change), or just the largest one?

questions.title: Implementation detail: Where exactly is \(\mathbf{R}\) applied inside Transformers and CNNs?
questions.question_body: For a pretrained linear layer with weights \(\mathbf{W}^0\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}\), BOFT uses \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0\). In practice, for MHA and MLP modules in Transformers, do we apply \(\mathbf{R}\) to the input dimension (rows) of all linear sub-layers (e.g., Q/K/V/O, and MLP in/out) or selectively? How are biases handled? Are there layers where applying \(\mathbf{R}\) harms performance or violates architectural constraints (e.g., layer norm placements)?

questions.title: How is backpropagation through a product of many orthogonal factors stabilized?
questions.question_body: BOFT stacks \(m\) orthogonal components, so gradients must pass through repeated multiplications of orthogonal blocks and their Cayley transforms. Does this cause vanishing/exploding gradients in practice? Are there known tricks (e.g., re-orthogonalization, parameter rescaling, skipping connections between factors) to stabilize training, especially for large \(m\)?

questions.title: BOFT vs. LoRA: When would low-rank additive updates be preferable to multiplicative orthogonal updates?
questions.question_body: Conceptually, LoRA learns a low-rank additive update \(\Delta\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}\), while BOFT learns a multiplicative orthogonal \(\mathbf{R}\). Are there scenarios where low-rank structure better matches the task’s inductive bias than near-isometric transformations? For example, if a task primarily needs to change the spectrum of \(\mathbf{W}^0\), would LoRA be more effective since BOFT preserves singular values?

questions.title: Clarifying the information-transmission graph: How do sparse patterns map to permutations between levels?
questions.question_body: The paper states each butterfly component \(\tilde{\mathbf{B}}(d,k)\) is a block-diagonal matrix whose nonzero pattern is a permutation of \(\tilde{\mathbf{B}}(d,2)\). Could you show explicitly, for \(d=8\), how the edges (nonzeros) of \(\tilde{\mathbf{B}}(8,4)\) can be obtained from permuting the blocks of \(\tilde{\mathbf{B}}(8,2)\)? A concrete mapping would help me understand the level-to-level connectivity evolution.

questions.title: Real vs. complex transforms: Can BOFT recover the DFT exactly using only real orthogonal factors?
questions.question_body: The FFT (DFT) is unitary and generally complex-valued. The paper claims butterfly structures can recover many classic fast transforms. When restricting BOFT to real orthogonal matrices, can we exactly recover the DFT (perhaps via a real-valued embedding of complex arithmetic), or only approximate it? If exact recovery is possible, what is the construction and parameterization required?

questions.title: What does the "weight interpolation" property mean concretely for BOFT?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions an "intriguing weight interpolation" due to matrix factorization (referencing a figure). Could someone explain explicitly how varying a subset of butterfly components between identity and learned values induces a continuous path from \(\mathbf{W}^0\) to \(\mathbf{R}\mathbf{W}^0\)? Is there an analytical expression showing this acts like a multi-stage homotopy, and does this have any practical training benefits (e.g., curriculum over \(m\))?

questions.title: Does composing many orthogonals increase training time significantly, and can we fuse them?
questions.question_body: The paper notes runtime overhead during training because \(\mathbf{R}\) is a product of \(m\) sparse factors. (1) What are the actual asymptotic and measured costs relative to LoRA and block-diagonal OFT? (2) Can we fuse consecutive butterfly components periodically during training to reduce overhead while keeping gradients correct (e.g., by treating the fused block as a single orthogonal with a cached factorization)?

questions.title: How does BOFT handle layers with different input/output dimensions (rectangular \(\mathbf{W}^0\))?
questions.question_body: The formulation uses \(\mathbf{W}^0\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}\) and left-multiplies by \(\mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\). For layers where \(d\neq n\) (e.g., projection up or down), is there any constraint on choosing \(d\) for \(\mathbf{R}\)? Do we ever need a right-multiplicative \(\mathbf{W}^0\mathbf{R}\) to affect the output channel interactions, and if so, how would BOFT be adapted while keeping orthogonality?

questions.title: Are there known failure cases where BOFT’s inductive bias hurts performance?
questions.question_body: The paper argues that butterfly structure provides a beneficial implicit bias tied to classic transforms. Are there tasks or layers where this structured prior is too restrictive (e.g., needs non-isometric scaling or highly localized, non-mixing changes)? Any empirical observations or diagnostics to detect when BOFT underfits due to its structure?

questions.title: Edge-case question: Does sparsity in \(\mathbf{W}^0\) interact poorly with BOFT’s dense mixing?
questions.question_body: If a pretrained layer \(\mathbf{W}^0\) is already sparse or has strong local structure (e.g., block-sparse), does left-multiplying by a dense orthogonal \(\mathbf{R}\) harm that structure in a way that degrades downstream performance or interpretability? Are there variants of BOFT that respect a given sparsity pattern (e.g., restricted permutations or masked butterfly factors)?

questions.title: Practical initialization: Is identity initialization sufficient when stacking many butterfly components?
questions.question_body: BOFT initializes each butterfly component as identity. With \(m=\log d\) or larger, could this create optimization issues (e.g., many layers initially doing nothing, leading to small gradients)? Have you tried small random skew-symmetric initializations in \(\mathbf{Q}\) or a warm-start schedule where components are unfrozen progressively?
